cases.name: l10n-qa-json
cases.promptMarkdown: Can you QA our Spanish strings before release? Buttons must fit 25 characters. B2B app, formal voice. en.json: ```json { "button.invite": "Invite teammate", "confirm.delete_body": "This will permanently remove {{count}} integrations from {{workspace}}.", "error.rate_limit": "You've hit the rate limit. Try again in {seconds} seconds.", "toast.welcome": "Welcome back, {name}.", "toast.invite_sent": "Invite sent to {email}!", "help.webhook": "Your endpoint must respond within 5 seconds." } ``` es.json: ```json { "button.invite": "Invitar a un compañero de equipo", "confirm.delete_body": "Esto eliminará permanentemente {{cuenta}} integraciones de {{workspace}}.", "error.rate_limit": "Alcanzó el límite de uso. Vuelva a intentarlo en {seconds} segundos.", "toast.welcome": "Te damos la bienvenida de nuevo, {name}.", "toast.invite_sent": "Invitación enviada a {email}!", "help.webhook": "Su endpoint debe responder en un máximo de 50 segundos." } ```

graders.name: finds-bugs
graders.graderMarkdown:

1. `{{cuenta}}` is a renamed placeholder; it must stay `{{count}}`.
2. The `<b>` tags around `{{workspace}}` were lost.
3. "Invitar a un compañero de equipo" is over the 25-character button limit, with a shorter suggestion.
4. "5 seconds" became "50 segundos".
5. The opening "¡" is missing in the invite toast.
6. "Te damos la bienvenida" uses tú while the rest of the file uses usted (formal voice requested).

FAIL if any of the six is missed, or if the reply suggests translating or renaming a placeholder.

graders.evidence: I found 6 issues. Two of them will break things at runtime and one gives users a wrong number, so these strings shouldn't ship as they are. ## Blockers | Key | Issue | Severity | |---|---|---| | `confirm.delete_body` | The placeholder `{{count}}` was translated to `{{cuenta}}`. Interpolation will fail, and users will see the literal `{{cuenta}}` or nothing. | Critical | | `confirm.delete_body` | The `…` tags around `{{workspace}}` were dropped, so the workspace name loses its bold formatting. | High | | `help.webhook` | **5 seconds became 50 seconds.** That's wrong technical guidance, and it will cause failed webhook integrations and support tickets. | Critical | | `button.invite` | "Invitar a un compañero de equipo" is **32 characters**, over the 25-character button limit. | High | ## Voice and style | Key | Issue | |---|---| | `toast.welcome` | "**Te** damos" uses informal *tú*. The other strings use formal *usted* ("Vuelva", "Su"), so this should be "**Le** damos". | | `toast.invite_sent` | It's missing the opening **¡**, which Spanish requires. | | `error.rate_limit` | No changes needed: formal voice is consistent and `{seconds}` is kept. | ## Corrected es.json ```json { "button.invite": "Invitar a un miembro", "confirm.delete_body": "Esto eliminará permanentemente {{count}} integraciones de {{workspace}}.", "error.rate_limit": "Alcanzó el límite de uso. Vuelva a intentarlo en {seconds} segundos.", "toast.welcome": "Le damos la bienvenida de nuevo, {name}.", "toast.invite_sent": "¡Invitación enviada a {email}!", "help.webhook": "Su endpoint debe responder en un máximo de 5 segundos." } ``` - **Button text:** "Invitar a un miembro" is 20 characters. It's also gender-neutral, which "compañero" isn't. If you'd prefer to stay closer to the source, "Invitar a un compañero" is 22 characters and also fits. ## Problems in the English source These need engineering to look at, and the fixes would apply to every locale: 1. **Two placeholder styles are mixed.** `confirm.delete_body` uses `{{count}}` while the other keys use `{name}`. Check that your i18n library handles both, because one style may be failing silently already. 2. **There's no plural handling in `confirm.delete_body`.** When count is 1 it renders "1 integrations" in English and "1 integraciones" in Spanish. Use plural keys, for example i18next's `_one`/`_other`: - `_one`: "Esto eliminará permanentemente {{count}} integración de {{workspace}}." - `_other`: "Esto eliminará permanentemente {{count}} integraciones de {{workspace}}." 3. **The same plural problem applies to `{seconds}`** in `error.rate_limit` ("1 segundos"). **Before release:** add an automated check to your pipeline that confirms placeholder names, HTML tags and numbers match between the source and each translation. Two of the blockers above, the renamed placeholder and 5 becoming 50, are the kind of error that check is designed to catch.

graders.name: finds-bugs
graders.evidence: I found 6 issues across the 6 strings: 3 will break things at runtime or mislead users, and 3 are formality or style problems. ## Blockers **1. `help.webhook`: the number is wrong** The Spanish says **50** seconds, but the source says **5**. Users would set up endpoints that time out. This is the most serious issue. ```json "help.webhook": "Su endpoint debe responder en un plazo máximo de 5 segundos." ``` **2. `confirm.delete_body`: renamed placeholder and missing markup** - `{{count}}` was translated to `{{cuenta}}`. It won't be filled in, so users will see the literal `{{cuenta}}` text (or an empty value) in a delete confirmation. - The `…` around `{{workspace}}` was dropped, so the workspace name won't be bold the way it is in English. ```json "confirm.delete_body": "Esto eliminará de forma permanente {{count}} integraciones de {{workspace}}." ``` **3. `button.invite`: too long** "Invitar a un compañero de equipo" is **32 characters**, over the 25 limit. ```json "button.invite": "Invitar al equipo" ``` That's 17 characters. "Invitar a un colega" (19) also works if you'd rather keep the person in the wording. ## Formal voice **4. `toast.welcome`: uses informal "tú"** "Te damos" is the informal form. Use formal *usted*, matching the other strings: ```json "toast.welcome": "Le damos la bienvenida de nuevo, {name}." ``` ## Punctuation and style **5. `toast.invite_sent`: missing opening "¡"** ```json "toast.invite_sent": "¡Invitación enviada a {email}!" ``` For a formal B2B tone you could also drop the exclamation: `"Invitación enviada a {email}."` **6. `error.rate_limit`: optional wording change** The placeholder and formality are correct. "Límite de uso" is understandable, but "límite de solicitudes" is the usual term for a rate limit: ```json "error.rate_limit": "Ha alcanzado el límite de solicitudes. Vuelva a intentarlo en {seconds} segundos." ``` ("Ha alcanzado" is neutral across regions. "Alcanzó" reads as Latin American, which is fine if that's your market.) ## Also worth fixing (in the English source too) - **Placeholder style is mixed.** `confirm.delete_body` uses `{{double}}` braces and every other string uses `{single}`. The Spanish copies the English, so it isn't a translation error, but check that your i18n library handles both styles. Otherwise one set won't interpolate in either language. - **No plural handling.** When the count is 1 you'll get "1 integraciones" and "1 segundos" (and "1 integrations" in English). If your library supports plural forms (ICU or i18next `_one`/`_other`), add them for `count` and `seconds`. ## Corrected es.json ```json { "button.invite": "Invitar al equipo", "confirm.delete_body": "Esto eliminará de forma permanente {{count}} integraciones de {{workspace}}.", "error.rate_limit": "Ha alcanzado el límite de solicitudes. Vuelva a intentarlo en {seconds} segundos.", "toast.welcome": "Le damos la bienvenida de nuevo, {name}.", "toast.invite_sent": "¡Invitación enviada a {email}!", "help.webhook": "Su endpoint debe responder en un plazo máximo de 5 segundos." } ```

cases.promptMarkdown: How do you say "good morning" in French?

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown: PASS if the reply says "bonjour". FAIL otherwise.

config.criteria: PASS if the reply says "bonjour". FAIL otherwise.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
"Good morning" in French is **"Bonjour"** (pronounced *bohn-ZHOOR*).

French has no separate phrase for "good morning." People use "bonjour" from morning until about late afternoon. In the evening they switch to **"Bonsoir"** (good evening).

graders.name: answer

"Good morning" in French is **"Bonjour"**.

French doesn't have a separate phrase for morning the way English does. "Bonjour" literally means "good day," and people use it from morning through late afternoon. In the evening they switch to **"Bonsoir"** ("good evening").

You may also see **"Bon matin,"** but that's mostly Québécois. In France, "Bonjour" is the normal choice.

Mexican legal terms with no exact US equivalent stay in Spanish in italics, with a short explanation the first time they appear.

[Seal of *Notario Público* No. 142]
[Signature of the appearing party]
[Signature and rubric of the Notary]

Date: <Month DD, YYYY>
Signature: ____________________

| Source | Target | Notes |
|---|---|---|

| Notario Público | *Notario Público* (explained on first use) | Not the same as a US notary public. Mexican notaries are attorneys with much broader legal authority. Translating it as plain "Notary Public" would mislead a US reader. |
| Licenciado | *Licenciado* (explained) | Academic and professional title with no direct English equivalent. |
| Comparece | There appears | Standard notarial formula for a party appearing before the notary. |
| Poder general amplísimo | Broadest general power of attorney | "Amplísimo" means the power covers all three categories in art. 2554. The Spanish is kept in brackets because banks often search for it. |
| Pleitos y cobranzas | Lawsuits and collections | Accepted rendering (art. 2554, ¶1). |
| Actos de administración | Acts of administration | Art. 2554, ¶2. |
| Actos de dominio | Acts of ownership | Art. 2554, ¶3: the power to dispose of or encumber the grantor's assets. "Acts of dominion" is also used. |

## Translator's notes

- **"Licenciado"** is kept as an honorific. It's a professional title for someone with a law degree, not a first name.
- **"Firma y rúbrica"** is translated as "signature and initials." The *rúbrica* is the flourish or paraph Mexican notaries add to their full signature.
- **"Actos de dominio"** is translated as "acts of ownership," with the Spanish kept in brackets. Some translators use "acts of dominion" or "acts of disposition." This is the power to sell, encumber or transfer the grantor's assets.

1. **"Notary Public number 142 of the Distrito Federal" in a 2024 deed.** The Distrito Federal became Ciudad de México in 2016, so a 2024 instrument would normally say "Notario Público número 142 de la Ciudad de México." I can give you an accurate translation, but **I can't certify it myself**. A US bank will expect a certification statement signed by a qualified human translator, and often notarized. Below is the translation, a certification statement a translator can review and sign, and some points the bank is likely to ask about.

---

## English Translation

**PUBLIC INSTRUMENT NUMBER 14,827**

In Mexico City, on the twelfth day of the month of March of the year two thousand twenty-four, BEFORE ME, Roberto Hernández Salinas, Esq. (*Licenciado*), Notary Public number 142 of the Federal District, there appears Mr. JUAN CARLOS RAMÍREZ DE LA VEGA, a Mexican national, of legal age, married, a businessman, a native and resident of this City, with an address for purposes of this instrument at Avenida Reforma number 250, 14th floor, Colonia Juárez, Postal Code 06600. He identifies himself with a voter identification card issued by the National Electoral Institute (*Instituto Nacional Electoral*), elector key RMVGJN85031509H701. He states that he has the legal capacity to contract and bind himself, and he hereby grants a BROADEST GENERAL POWER OF ATTORNEY (*PODER GENERAL AMPLÍSIMO*) for lawsuits and collections, acts of administration, and acts of ownership, in favor of Mrs. MARÍA ELENA TORRES NÚÑEZ, under the terms of article two thousand five hundred fifty-four of the Civil Code for the Federal District.

[Seal of Notary Public 142]
[Signature of the appearing party]
[Signature and initials (*rúbrica*) of the Notary]

---

## Translator's Notes

1. **"Distrito Federal" in 2024.** The Federal District was officially renamed Ciudad de México (Mexico City) in 2016. The deed itself says "Ciudad de México," but it calls the notary "Notario Público número 142 *del Distrito Federal*." I translated this as written. A 2024 notary would normally be styled "of Mexico City," so the bank may want to check the notary's registration with the Colegio de Notarios de la Ciudad de México. The name "Código Civil para el Distrito Federal" is still commonly cited, so that reference isn't unusual.
2. **"Poder general amplísimo… actos de dominio."** This is the broadest form of general power under Article 2554. "Acts of ownership" (*actos de dominio*) means the attorney-in-fact can dispose of the principal's assets, for example by selling, encumbering or transferring them, as if she were the owner.
3. **"Rúbrica"** is a stylized flourish or initials that goes with a signature in Mexican notarial practice. I rendered it as "initials" and kept the Spanish term.
4. Numbers and dates that are written out in words in the original are also written out in words in the translation, as is customary for notarial instruments.

## Certification Statement (for the translator to review and sign)

> I, [Full Name], certify that I am competent to translate from Spanish into English, and that the foregoing is a true, complete, and accurate translation of the attached document titled "Escritura Pública Número 14,827," to the best of my knowledge and ability.
>
> Signature: ____________________
> Date: ____________________
> Address / Contact: ____________________
> [Credentials, e.g., ATA-certified, if applicable]

The translator should compare this against the source before signing; certification means they take responsibility for it. Many banks also want the statement notarized.

## Points the bank may raise

- **This is an excerpt.** Banks usually want the full instrument. The full deed may include limiting clauses, notarial certifications, and the date of the notary's authorization.
- **This is an individual power of attorney.** It gives Ms. Torres Núñez authority to act for Mr. Ramírez de la Vega personally, not for a company. If the bank needs to confirm that she can sign for a business entity, they will need that entity's corporate powers.
- **An apostille** (Hague Convention) on the original deed is usually needed before it's accepted in the US.
- **Revocation:** Mexican powers of attorney can be revoked, so the bank may ask for a recent certified copy or confirmation that the power is still in force.

cases.name: rae-dequeismo
cases.promptMarkdown: ¿Es correcto decir "pienso de que deberíamos lanzar la versión en español el lunes"? Lo vi en un correo de un cliente.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if the reply, in Spanish, identifies "pienso de que" as dequeísmo, gives "pienso que" as the correct form, and either cites a DPD/RAE source or clearly says the claim could not be verified online.
FAIL if it calls "pienso de que" correct, gives no correction, or claims "the RAE says" without a source and without saying it is unverified.

config.criteria:
PASS if the reply, in Spanish, identifies "pienso de que" as dequeísmo, gives "pienso que" as the correct form, and either cites a DPD/RAE source or clearly says the claim could not be verified online.
FAIL if it calls "pienso de que" correct, gives no correction, or claims "the RAE says" without a source and without saying it is unverified.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
No, no es correcto. Es un caso de **dequeísmo**, que consiste en poner un *de* delante de *que* sin que la gramática lo pida. Lo correcto es:

> **Pienso que** deberíamos lanzar la versión en español el lunes.

**Por qué:** lo que sigue a *pienso* es el complemento directo del verbo, y según el *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* (DPD) el complemento directo nunca lleva *de* delante. De hecho, el DPD pone «pienso de que…» como ejemplo principal de este error. Lo mismo ocurre con otros verbos de pensamiento y de lengua: *creo que*, *opino que*, *me dijeron que*.

**Truco para comprobarlo** (del *Libro de estilo* de la RAE): cambia la parte que empieza por *que* por «eso».
- «Pienso **eso**» funciona, pero «pienso de eso» no. Por tanto, no lleva *de*.
- «Me alegro **de eso**» sí lleva *de*. Por tanto, «me alegro **de** que…» es correcto, y quitar el *de* ahí sería el error contrario (queísmo).

**Matiz:** *pensar de* sí es correcto cuando significa «tener una opinión sobre algo», como en «¿Qué piensas **de** la nueva versión?». Lo que no admite es *de* delante de *que* cuando lo que sigue es lo que se piensa.

Como viene de un cliente, yo no lo corregiría. Es un error frecuente al hablar, aunque el DPD lo desaconseja en el habla culta. Si vas a citar o reutilizar la frase en algún texto vuestro, usa «pienso que».

**Fuentes:**
- [DPD: dequeísmo](https://www.rae.es/dpd/deque%C3%ADsmo)
- [RAE, *Libro de estilo*: queísmo, dequeísmo y deísmo](https://www.rae.es/libro-estilo-lengua-espa%C3%B1ola/que%C3%ADsmo-deque%C3%ADsmo-y-de%C3%ADsmo)

(La página del DPD me devolvió un error de acceso, así que lo verifiqué con el resumen del buscador de esa misma entrada y del *Libro de estilo*).

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
No, no es correcto. Es un caso de **dequeísmo**: se pone *de* delante de *que* donde la gramática no lo pide. Lo correcto es:

> **Pienso que deberíamos lanzar la versión en español el lunes.**

**Por qué está mal:** según el *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas*, es un error poner *de* delante de una oración que funciona como complemento directo. *Pensar* lleva complemento directo (se piensa *algo*), y el complemento directo nunca va introducido por *de*. El propio DPD pone casi esta misma frase como ejemplo de error: «Pienso de que…». Pasa lo mismo con *creer*, *opinar*, *considerar*, *decir* o *temer*.

**Truco para comprobarlo:** cambia la parte que empieza por *que* por *eso*.
- «Pienso **eso**» suena bien, pero «Pienso **de eso**» no. Por tanto, *pienso que*.
- «Me alegro **de eso**» sí funciona. Por tanto, *me alegro **de** que…* es correcto, y quitarle el *de* sería el error contrario (queísmo).

**Un detalle:** «pensar **en** algo» existe y es correcto («Pienso en que deberíamos…»), pero significa «tener en mente», no «opinar». En el correo de tu cliente lo natural es simplemente *pienso que*.

Es un error muy común en la lengua hablada de toda Latinoamérica y España. Si vas a responder al cliente, no hace falta comentárselo. Pero si esa frase va a acabar en algún texto publicado, conviene corregirla.

No pude abrir la página del DPD directamente porque el sitio de la RAE bloqueó el acceso (error 403). Lo comprobé a través de los resultados de búsqueda que citan la entrada.

Fuentes:
- [DPD – dequeísmo (RAE)](https://www.rae.es/dpd/deque%C3%ADsmo)
- [Libro de estilo de la lengua española – Queísmo, dequeísmo y deísmo (RAE)](https://www.rae.es/libro-estilo-lengua-espa%C3%B1ola/que%C3%ADsmo-deque%C3%ADsmo-y-de%C3%ADsmo)

> **Pienso que** deberíamos lanzar la versión en español el lunes.

**Por qué:** lo que se piensa es el complemento directo de *pensar*, y el complemento directo nunca lleva *de*. El *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* da *«Pienso de que conseguiremos ganar el campeonato»* como uno de sus ejemplos de este error. Fuentes:
- [DPD: dequeísmo (rae.es)](https://www.rae.es/dpd/deque%C3%ADsmo)
- [Libro de estilo de la lengua española: queísmo, dequeísmo y deísmo (rae.es)](https://www.rae.es/libro-estilo-lengua-espa%C3%B1ola/que%C3%ADsmo-deque%C3%ADsmo-y-de%C3%ADsmo)

**Forma correcta:**
> *Pienso que deberíamos lanzar la versión en español el lunes.*

**Por qué:** cuando *pensar* significa "creer" u "opinar", es transitivo. Lo que se piensa es el complemento directo, y el complemento directo no lleva *de*.

**Truco para comprobarlo:** sustituye la oración que empieza por *que* por *eso*:
- *Pienso eso.* ✅ → por tanto, *pienso que…*
- *Pienso de eso.* ❌

**Ojo:** *pensar de* sí es correcto cuando significa "tener una opinión sobre algo":
- *¿Qué piensas **de** la nueva versión?* ✅

Si vas a responder al cliente, no hace falta corregirle. Es un error muy frecuente en el habla, aunque en textos formales o traducciones conviene evitarlo.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
No, no es correcto según la norma. Es un caso de **dequeísmo**, es decir, poner un *de* que sobra delante de *que*.

**Forma correcta:**
> Pienso que deberíamos lanzar la versión en español el lunes.

**Por qué:** cuando *pensar* significa "opinar" o "creer", lleva un complemento directo sin preposición. Se dice "pienso algo", no "pienso de algo".

**Truco para comprobarlo:** sustituye la oración que empieza por *que* por *eso*:
- "Pienso **eso**" → suena bien, así que va sin *de*: *pienso que…* ✅
- "Pienso **de eso**" → no tiene sentido, así que *pienso de que* ❌

**Ojo, hay construcciones parecidas que sí son correctas:**
- **Pensar en**, con el sentido de "tener en mente": *Pienso en que el lunes hay mucho tráfico.*
- **Pensar de**, para pedir u opinar sobre algo: *¿Qué piensas de la propuesta?* Aquí *de* va delante de un sustantivo, no de una oración con *que*.

El dequeísmo es muy común en el habla de muchos países, así que no es raro verlo en un correo. Si vas a citar o adaptar ese texto para la versión en español, conviene corregirlo a *pienso que*.

graders.evidence:

Lo correcto es:

> **Pienso que** deberíamos lanzar la versión en español el lunes.

**Por qué:** cuando "pensar" significa "opinar" o "creer", va directamente con lo que se piensa. Se piensa *algo*, no *de algo*.

**Truco para comprobarlo:** cambia todo lo que va desde "que" hasta el final por "eso":
- "Pienso **eso**" ✅ → se escribe "pienso que..."
- "Pienso **de eso**" ❌ → no lleva "de"

**Ojo con estos casos, que sí son correctos:**
- "¿Qué piensas **de** la propuesta?" ✅ Aquí "pensar de" significa "tener una opinión sobre algo" y va seguido de un sustantivo, no de una oración con "que".
- "Me acordé **de que** era lunes" ✅ El verbo es "acordarse de algo", así que el "de" sí corresponde. Si lo quitas, el error es el contrario y se llama **queísmo**.

Este error es muy común en el habla de muchos países, así que en un correo de un cliente no vale la pena comentarlo. Pero si vas a citar o reutilizar esa frase en un texto formal o publicado, usa "pienso que".

cases.name: renewal-email-en-to-es-latam
cases.promptMarkdown:
Translate this customer success email to Spanish for our LATAM enterprise customers. The recipient is a Director of Operations at a logistics company in Colombia. We have a formal relationship — they're a paying customer renewing a $180K annual contract.

---

Subject: Your renewal is coming up — quick proposal inside

Hi Andrés,

I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to reach out personally because your contract with us is up for renewal on June 15th, and based on the conversations our team has had with yours over the past quarter, I think there's a meaningful opportunity to expand the partnership.

Three things on my mind:

1. Your team has driven a 40% increase in API call volume over the last six months — well beyond what your current tier supports. We should level you up before you hit the ceiling.

2. The new analytics dashboard we shipped in Q1 isn't available on your plan, but your operations team would get real value from it. Happy to comp you a 90-day trial as part of the renewal.

3. I'd like to lock in your current per-seat rate for another two years before the price increase takes effect in September.

Could you spare 20 minutes next week to walk through this together? I'm flexible Tuesday through Thursday.

Looking forward to it.

Best,
Claire Bennett
Senior Account Executive, Customer Success

FAIL if any fact is missing, changed, softened or added.

graders.name: faithful
graders.evidence:
# Translation: Customer success renewal email (EN → ES)

## Register & audience analysis
This is a B2B renewal and upsell email to a Director of Operations at a Colombian logistics company, on a $180K contract. I used **usted** throughout, as you'd expect for a formal enterprise relationship. "Ustedes" is used where the email means the customer's whole team or company. The source is warm and direct ("Hi Andrés," "Three things on my mind," "level you up"), so I kept it friendly but toned the casual phrases up to match a professional Colombian business register. The opener is shorter, which is normal in Spanish business email. I chose some wording that suits Colombia, since the recipient is known.

## Translation

**Asunto:** Se acerca su renovación: le comparto una breve propuesta

Cordial saludo, Andrés:

Espero que se encuentre muy bien. Quería escribirle personalmente porque la renovación de su contrato con nosotros está prevista para el 15 de junio y, a partir de las conversaciones que nuestro equipo ha tenido con el suyo durante el último trimestre, considero que existe una oportunidad significativa para ampliar nuestra alianza.

Hay tres puntos que quisiera plantearle:

1. En los últimos seis meses, su equipo ha generado un aumento del 40% en el volumen de llamadas a la API, muy por encima de lo que admite su nivel actual. Conviene que pasemos a un nivel superior antes de que lleguen al límite.

2. El nuevo panel de análisis que lanzamos en el primer trimestre no está incluido en su plan, pero su equipo de operaciones le sacaría mucho provecho. Con gusto puedo ofrecerles una prueba de cortesía de 90 días como parte de la renovación.

3. Me gustaría congelar su tarifa actual por licencia durante dos años más, antes de que el aumento de precios entre en vigor en septiembre.

¿Podría dedicarme 20 minutos la próxima semana para revisar juntos estos puntos? Tengo disponibilidad de martes a jueves.

Quedo a la espera de su respuesta.

Cordialmente,

Claire Bennett
Senior Account Executive, Customer Success

## Glossary of key terms

| Source | Target | Notes |

# Translation: API integration platform UI strings (EN → ES, neutral Latin American Spanish)

## Register & audience analysis
These are UI strings for a B2B developer platform, read by engineering managers and senior developers. To match the clinical, formal voice you described, I used *usted*. Where possible I used impersonal *se* constructions ("Se eliminarán…", "Se alcanzó…") so the text doesn't address the reader directly. Buttons use bare infinitives, which is the standard for formal Spanish UI. I kept English the technical terms that Spanish-speaking developers normally leave in English (*endpoint*, *webhook*, *API*, *stack*).

## Translation
```json
{
  "button.save": "Guardar cambios",
  "button.delete": "Eliminar",
  "button.cancel": "Cancelar",
  "button.invite": "Invitar a un miembro",
  "confirm.delete.title": "¿Eliminar {{count}} integraciones?",
  "confirm.delete.body": "Se eliminarán de forma permanente {{count}} integraciones de su espacio de trabajo. Esta acción no se puede deshacer.",
  "error.rate_limit": "Se alcanzó el límite de solicitudes. Vuelva a intentarlo en {{seconds}} segundos.",
  "empty_state.title": "Aún no hay integraciones",
  "empty_state.body": "Conecte su primera API para comenzar a sincronizar datos en todo su stack tecnológico.",
  "toast.invite_sent": "Invitación enviada a {{email}}",
  "webhook.help": "El endpoint de su webhook debe devolver un código 2xx en 5 segundos o menos.",
  "settings.api_key.label": "Clave de API",
  "settings.api_key.help": "Use esta clave en el encabezado Authorization de sus solicitudes."
}
```

## Glossary of key terms
| Source | Target | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| integration | integración | Same word in every string |
| workspace | espacio de trabajo | Use this everywhere in the product |
| delete / remove | eliminar | One verb for both. *Remover* is a false friend (it means "to stir") |
| rate limit | límite de solicitudes | More precise for an API than *límite de uso*. See note 4 |
| request | solicitud | Standard in UI text |
| API key | clave de API | Standard term across Latin America |
| header | encabezado | See note 6 |
| endpoint, webhook, API, stack | kept in English | These are the established terms in Spanish developer writing |
| teammate | miembro | See note 1 |

## Translator's notes
1. **"Invite teammate"**: The literal "Invitar a un compañero de equipo" is 32 characters, over your 25-character limit. I used "Invitar a un miembro" (20). *Miembro* is the same for any gender and reads clearly when you're in a workspace. Another option is "Invitar a colaborador" (21), but *colaborador* is grammatically masculine.
2. **`{{count}}` plurals**: Both confirmation strings assume more than one integration. If `count` can be 1, "¿Eliminar 1 integraciones?" will be wrong, just as "Delete 1 integrations?" is wrong in English. I recommend ICU plural syntax, for example `{count, plural, one {¿Eliminar # integración?} other {¿Eliminar # integraciones?}}`. The body string would need the same treatment.
3. **Formal address**: Imperatives use *usted* ("Conecte", "Use", "Vuelva a intentarlo"). Two strings use impersonal constructions to keep the tone clinical rather than personal ("You've hit the rate limit" became "Se alcanzó el límite…").
4. **"rate limit"**: Some teams keep "rate limit" in English in their docs. If your Spanish documentation already does that, change this string to match.
5. **"webhook.help"**: My first version was 1.4× the English length, so I shortened it. "Within 5 seconds" became "en 5 segundos o menos", which keeps the meaning of "up to 5 seconds". I also shortened "código de estado 2xx" to "código 2xx", which senior developers will read without trouble. If you have room, "código de estado 2xx" is slightly more precise.
6. **"Authorization header"**: The header name stays exactly as written because it's a literal identifier. For "header" itself I used *encabezado*, which Spanish-language references such as MDN use. If your docs say "header", use that here too. Consider showing `Authorization` in code formatting if the UI supports it.
7. **"across your stack"**: I wrote "en todo su stack tecnológico". If you'd rather avoid the anglicism, "en todos sus sistemas" also works.

**QA:** I ran the `l10n-qa` checker on the final file, with a 25-character limit on buttons and 40 on confirmation titles. It found 0 errors and 0 warnings. All placeholders are intact, every key is present, and all buttons are within the limit (longest: "Invitar a un miembro", 20 characters).

# Translation: UI strings for an API-integration developer platform (EN → ES, neutral LatAm)

## Register & audience analysis
These are UI strings for a B2B developer product, read by engineering managers and senior developers. I used formal *usted* throughout (*Conecte*, *Vuelva a intentarlo*, *su espacio de trabajo*). Where the English allows it, I used impersonal constructions (*Se eliminarán…*, *Se alcanzó…*), which give the clinical, Stripe-like voice you asked for. There's no *por favor*, no exclamation marks and no warm filler. Standard developer terms (*endpoint*, *webhook*, *stack*, `Authorization`, `2xx`) stay in English, as Spanish-speaking developers expect.

## Translation

```json
{
  "button.save": "Guardar cambios",
  "button.delete": "Eliminar",
  "button.cancel": "Cancelar",
  "button.invite": "Invitar a un miembro",
  "confirm.delete.title": "¿Eliminar {{count}} integraciones?",
  "confirm.delete.body": "Se eliminarán de forma permanente {{count}} integraciones de su espacio de trabajo. Esta acción no se puede deshacer.",
  "error.rate_limit": "Se alcanzó el límite de solicitudes. Vuelva a intentarlo en {{seconds}} segundos.",
  "empty_state.title": "Aún no hay integraciones",
  "empty_state.body": "Conecte su primera API para comenzar a sincronizar datos en todo su stack.",
  "toast.invite_sent": "Invitación enviada a {{email}}",
  "webhook.help": "El endpoint de su webhook debe devolver un código de estado 2xx en 5 segundos o menos.",
  "settings.api_key.label": "Clave de API",
  "settings.api_key.help": "Use esta clave en el encabezado Authorization de sus solicitudes."
}
```

## Glossary of key terms

| Source | Target | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Delete / remove | Eliminar | Used for both the button and the body text so the action is named consistently. Avoids the false friend *remover* ("to stir"). |
| Integration | Integración | |
| Workspace | Espacio de trabajo | Use it the same way everywhere else in the product. |
| Teammate | Miembro | *Miembro* is the same word for any gender, which avoids *compañero/a*. |
| Rate limit | Límite de solicitudes | See note 3. |
| Request | Solicitud | Matches *límite de solicitudes*. |
| Header | Encabezado | See note 5. |
| API key | Clave de API | The standard LatAm term (Google and AWS use it). |
| Endpoint, webhook, stack | Unchanged | These are the settled terms in Spanish developer writing. |
| Status code | Código de estado | |

## Translator's notes

1. **Length check.** I ran the l10n-qa checker with a 25-character limit on buttons. It finds no errors or warnings, and every placeholder (`{{count}}` ×2, `{{seconds}}`, `{{email}}`) is unchanged. The longest button is *Invitar a un miembro* at 20 characters.
2. **`confirm.delete.title` is 34 characters**, against 30 for the English. With a 25-character cap on titles it fails, but the English source already goes over 25, so I treated "roughly the same as English" as the target. I didn't switch to *Borrar*, which would save 2 characters but break consistency with the *Eliminar* button. If titles have a hard 25-character limit, I'd suggest a shorter fallback: *¿Eliminar integraciones?* (24), with the count moved to the body text.
3. **"rate limit"** became *límite de solicitudes*, which is clear to managers and developers alike. Many LatAm developers also say *rate limit*. Switch to that if your API docs keep the English term.
4. **Plurals.** `{{count}}` and `{{seconds}}` are plural-only, both in the source and in Spanish. With 1 they would show "¿Eliminar 1 integraciones?" and "1 segundos". I'd recommend ICU plural forms for these keys, e.g. `{count, plural, one {¿Eliminar # integración?} other {¿Eliminar # integraciones?}}`.
5. **"Authorization header"** became *encabezado Authorization*. MDN in Spanish and Stripe's Spanish docs both use *encabezado*. The header name itself stays in English because it's a literal token. Some teams prefer *header Authorization*, so make it match your docs.
6. **"within 5 seconds"** became *en 5 segundos o menos*. This keeps the inclusive meaning (≤ 5 s) and is shorter than *en un plazo máximo de*. I shortened it after the checker warned that my first version was 1.4× the English length.
7. **"across your stack"** became *en todo su stack*. If you want a fully Spanish wording for less technical readers, *en todos sus sistemas* works.
8. **"Invite sent"** became *Invitación enviada*. Spanish has no direct equivalent of the clipped noun "invite", so the full noun is the natural form.

**Decisions to review**
1. **`button.invite` → "Invitar al equipo".** A literal *"Invitar a un compañero"* (22 characters) fits the limit. But *compañero* is grammatically masculine, and *compañero/a* looks awkward on a button. "Invitar al equipo" avoids gender and is common SaaS wording.
